newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan says Fed may act before inflation worse.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan says Fed may act before inflation worse.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday repeated that the central bank may have to raise rates in anticipation of inflation rather than waiting before prices actually worsen.
In testimony before the Senate Banking Committee, Greenspan also said that wage increases alone are not necessarily a signal that inflation pressures are worsening.

"It is conceivable that that may require, because of the long lead times of certain types of policies actions, that we may decide because we think it's appropriate to have to move before you see actual evidences of real inflation emerging," he said.
But he made clear that upward pressure on wages is not necessarily a signal that inflation is emerging.

"I should emphasize that wages per se are not in and of themselves an issue of (inflation)," he said, adding: "If wages are rising and productivity is matching it, clearly that is not something that is destabalizing the economy."

Greenspan added that he saw no signs that consumption was rising faster than real incomes. "There is no evidence consumption is rising at a pace significantly different from the pace of real incomes," he said.

Asked about the extent to which he was concerned about the rise in credit card delinquencies, Greenspan said it was a problem for some individual households. But he played down the risks to the economy as a whole.
"It's not a macroeconomic problem in the sense that it's threatening to have a significant effect on banks generally or on the financial system," he said.
The Fed chief said banks appeared to be acting appropriately in pulling back on the extension of credit card debt.
Greenspan repeated his opposition to a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution. "I'm not in favor of a balanced budget amendment," he said.
But he said he did not see any reason why any particular spending program, including Social Security, would be put at risk from a balanced budget amendment.

The Fed chief, however, made clear that he was in favor of balancing the budget, saying that would help boost U.S. savings. "Eliminating the deficit is ... a very important element in overall economic policy," he said.
